title: Decode a medical word
outcome: Follow one word from components to precise meaning.

terms.definition: Inflammation of the pericardium, the sac around the heart.
Inflammation of the stomach lining.
Surgical removal of all or part of a kidney.
A procedure that widens a narrowed or obstructed blood vessel.

caution: Use suffix → root → prefix as a reading aid. The full clinical definition takes priority.
question: Which part of pericarditis means inflammation?
answer: -itis is the inflammation ending. The specific clinical structure is the pericardium.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 1, printed p. 2–15.

title: Build a vocabulary that lasts
outcome: Move from recognition to recall, spelling and explanation.

terms.definition: The subjective experience of difficult or uncomfortable breathing.
A lower-than-expected oxygen level in arterial blood.

parts.meaning: below or deficient (a form of hypo-)

terms.definition: An acquired impairment of language expression or comprehension.
Difficulty swallowing.

caution: Study one meaning, retrieve it without looking, check spelling, and use a fictional example.
question: Why are saved and self-rated familiar different from a correct answer?
answer: Saving and familiarity are personal choices; an exercise records an actual response.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 2, printed p. 16–27.

title: Prefixes that change the message
outcome: Compare amount, speed, location and time.

terms.definition: above normal or excessive
below normal or deficient
around
within

caution: A prefix modifies meaning. These examples are a selection, not a frequency-ranked top list.
question: Which means around: peri- or intra-?
answer: Peri- means around. Intra- means within.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, 3rd ed., Chapters 1–2 and relevant body-system chapters; MedlinePlus word-parts reference.

title: Read the ending first
outcome: Separate conditions, procedures, pain and examination.

terms.definition: inflammation
surgical removal
visual examination with an instrument
pain

caution: Similar endings can identify different concepts. Do not infer a diagnosis from a suffix alone.
question: How do -itis and -ectomy differ?
answer: -itis indicates inflammation; -ectomy indicates surgical removal.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, 3rd ed., Chapters 1–2 and relevant body-system chapters; MedlinePlus word-parts reference.

title: Direction and position in clinical language
outcome: Use paired spatial concepts to interpret a description.

terms.definition: Towards the front of the body in anatomical position.
Towards the back of the body in anatomical position.
Nearer to the point of attachment or origin.
Further from the point of attachment or origin.

caution: Orient descriptions to anatomical position. Proximal and distal require a reference point.
question: Which is nearer a limb attachment: proximal or distal?
answer: Proximal means nearer the point of attachment or origin.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 3, printed p. 28–46.

title: Musculoskeletal words in focus
outcome: Separate pain, inflammation, bone and muscle concepts.

terms.definition: Pain in a joint.
Inflammation of a joint or joints.
Pain in a muscle or muscles.
Reduced bone strength associated with low bone mass and structural deterioration.

caution: A body-part root locates the concept; the ending helps identify the process.
question: Do arthralgia and arthritis have the same meaning?
answer: No. Joint pain and joint inflammation are different concepts.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 47–79.

title: Skin words by layer and task
outcome: Connect location, inflammation, appearance and sampling.

terms.definition: Inflammation of the skin.
Situated or administered beneath the skin.
Redness of the skin.
Removal of cells or tissue for examination.

caution: An appearance term, a location term and a procedure term serve different purposes in a note.
question: Is subcutaneous a diagnosis or a location descriptor?
answer: It describes location beneath the skin.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 5, printed p. 80–107.

title: Blood terminology without confusion
outcome: Keep cell names, cell counts and haemostasis distinct.

terms.definition: A red blood cell.
A white blood cell.
A reduced platelet count in the blood.
The physiological process that stops bleeding.

caution: A cell name differs from a finding about its count or function.
question: Which term identifies a low platelet count?
answer: Thrombocytopenia.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 108–134.

title: Lymphatic and immune word map
outcome: Distinguish structures, enlargement and immune concepts.

terms.definition: Abnormality of lymph nodes, commonly enlargement.
Enlargement of the spleen.
White cell type including B, T and natural killer cells.
Reduced ability of the immune system to defend against infection.

caution: A term may identify an enlarged structure without identifying its cause.
question: Does splenomegaly alone establish the cause of enlargement?
answer: No. The word identifies spleen enlargement, not the cause.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 135–152.

title: Endocrine modifiers and measurements
outcome: Compare high and low, gland and blood findings.

terms.definition: A blood glucose concentration above the appropriate range.
A blood glucose concentration below the appropriate range.
A state of insufficient thyroid hormone action, usually from reduced production.
Relating to hormones released into the circulation by glands or specialised cells.

caution: Read the modifier and the measured concept together. A single word does not supply missing clinical context.
question: Which modifier in hypoglycaemia means low or deficient?
answer: Hypo-.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 153–179.

title: Cardiac words and affected structures
outcome: Separate rate, tissue inflammation and procedures.

terms.definition: A heart rate faster than expected for the clinical context.
Inflammation of the heart muscle.
Inflammation of the pericardium, the sac around the heart.
A procedure that widens a narrowed or obstructed blood vessel.

caution: A heart-rate description is not the same as inflammation of a cardiac structure.
question: Which identifies inflammation of heart muscle: myocarditis or pericarditis?
answer: Myocarditis.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 180–211.

title: Breathing is not the same as oxygenation
outcome: Distinguish breathlessness, rate, blood oxygen and tissue oxygen.

terms.definition: The subjective experience of difficult or uncomfortable breathing.
An increased breathing rate for the relevant age and context.
A lower-than-expected oxygen level in arterial blood.

parts.meaning: below or deficient (a form of hypo-)

terms.definition: Insufficient oxygen availability at the tissue level.

parts.meaning: below or deficient (a form of hypo-)

caution: The presence of breathlessness alone does not establish a blood oxygen finding.
question: Which term concerns low oxygen in arterial blood?
answer: Hypoxaemia.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 212–240.

title: Digestive terms from meaning to procedure
outcome: Identify swallowing, lining inflammation, examination and removal.

terms.definition: Difficulty swallowing.
Inflammation of the stomach lining.
Endoscopic examination of the upper digestive tract, including the stomach.
Surgical removal of the gallbladder.

caution: Distinguish a symptom from an examination and an operation.
question: Does dysphagia mean a language problem?
answer: No. Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing; language impairment is a different concept.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 241–271.

title: Neurological words with precise boundaries
outcome: Compare pain, nerve disease, paralysis and language impairment.

terms.definition: Pain along the distribution of a nerve.
Disease or dysfunction of one or more nerves.
Paralysis affecting one side of the body.
An acquired impairment of language expression or comprehension.

caution: Preserve the specific function and location described by the term.
question: Which term concerns language impairment?
answer: Aphasia.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 12, printed p. 272–299.

title: The senses and their word roots
outcome: Connect ear, eye and nose terminology.

terms.definition: Inflammation of the ear.
The medical specialty concerned with the eyes and vision.
Discharge from the nose.
Visual examination of the ear canal and eardrum.

caution: Body-part roots guide orientation; verify whether the term is a finding, specialty or examination.
question: Does otoscopy mean ear inflammation?
answer: No. Otoscopy is examination; otitis is inflammation.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 300–330.

title: Urinary words that look alike
outcome: Separate blood, pain, amount, stones and examination.

terms.definition: Blood in the urine.
Pain or discomfort during urination.
A reduced volume of urine output.
Visual examination of the bladder and urethra using a scope.

caution: Urine findings and urinary symptoms do not by themselves identify an underlying cause.
question: Which refers to a low urine volume?
answer: Oliguria.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 14, printed p. 331–357.

title: Male reproductive language
outcome: Identify structure, inflammation and surgery.

terms.definition: Inflammation of a testis.
Surgical removal of all or part of the prostate.
Gland surrounding the proximal urethra and contributing seminal fluid.
Gonad producing sperm and testosterone.

caution: A procedure name may not specify extent or indication; do not fill in missing details.
question: Does prostatectomy alone specify whether removal is partial or radical?
answer: No. Check the procedure documentation for its extent.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 15, printed p. 358–377.

title: Female reproductive procedures
outcome: Keep uterus, tubes and ovaries conceptually separate.

terms.definition: Surgical removal of the uterus.
Surgical removal of a fallopian tube or tubes.
Surgical removal of an ovary or ovaries.
Gonad producing oocytes and reproductive hormones.

caution: Do not assume that removing one structure means another was also removed.
question: Does hysterectomy alone confirm ovary removal?
answer: No. It identifies uterine removal; verify any additional procedure separately.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 378–400.

title: Pregnancy and newborn terminology
outcome: Use time labels and pregnancy-history words carefully.

terms.definition: Relating to the period before birth.
Relating to the newborn period, usually the first 28 days after birth.
A person who is pregnant for the first time.
Number of pregnancies a person has had.

caution: Gravidity and parity count different aspects of pregnancy history. Verify the documented history.
question: Which term identifies a first pregnancy?
answer: Primigravida.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 401–428.

title: Mental health language with care
outcome: Distinguish an observed symptom from broader clinical interpretation.

terms.definition: Difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or waking too early.
Reduced ability to experience interest or pleasure.
A sustained subjective emotional state.
Observable expression of emotion.

caution: Use person-respecting wording. A symptom term alone does not establish a diagnosis.
question: Which term concerns reduced ability to experience pleasure?
answer: Anhedonia.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 429–451.

title: Oncology terms and what they do not imply
outcome: Separate growth, behaviour and spread.

terms.definition: Abnormal new tissue growth.
Non-malignant; a benign tumour does not invade surrounding tissue or metastasise.
Describing cancer with the ability to invade tissue and potentially spread.
Spread of cancer from its original site to another part of the body.

caution: The ending -oma does not by itself establish whether a growth is malignant.
question: Are all neoplasms malignant?
answer: No. A neoplasm may be benign or malignant.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 452–474.

title: Infection terminology in context
outcome: Distinguish organism, presence in blood and clinical syndrome.

terms.definition: An organism or agent capable of causing disease.
The presence of bacteria in the bloodstream.
Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
Invasion and multiplication of an infectious agent with a host response.

caution: Bacteraemia and sepsis are not interchangeable; a term alone does not replace clinical assessment.
question: Do bacteraemia and sepsis mean the same thing?
answer: No. They describe different concepts.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 20, printed p. 475–494.

title: Imaging words and the resulting record
outcome: Compare image-production processes and examination methods.

terms.definition: The process of creating images using X-rays.
Image produced using X-rays.
Imaging that represents sections or slices of the body.
Imaging with high-frequency sound waves.

caution: The name of a test does not state its findings. Keep the process and the resulting image distinct.
question: Which is a resulting image: radiography or radiograph?
answer: Radiograph.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 21, printed p. 495–512.

title: Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics
outcome: Distinguish the body handling a medicine from its effects.

terms.definition: The study of how the body absorbs, distributes, metabolises and eliminates a medicine.
The study of a medicine’s effects and how those effects occur.
Circumstance in which an intervention should not be used.
The fraction of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged.

caution: This board teaches terminology, not drug choice or dosing.
question: Which term concerns what the body does to a medicine?
answer: Pharmacokinetics.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 22, printed p. 513–531.

title: Complementary alternative and integrative
outcome: Clarify how an approach is used, without claiming effectiveness.

terms.definition: An approach used alongside conventional medical care.
An approach used in place of conventional medical care.
Coordinated approach bringing conventional and complementary approaches together.
Use of plant-derived preparations for health-related purposes.

caution: Use alongside conventional care differs from use instead of it. A category label does not prove benefit or safety.
question: Which label describes use alongside conventional care?
answer: Complementary.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 23, printed p. 532–536.

title: Incidence prevalence and study questions
outcome: Separate new cases, existing cases and research designs.

terms.definition: The occurrence of new cases in a population at risk over a specified period.
The proportion of a population with a condition at a specified time or during a defined period.
A defined group of people followed or studied over time.
Study measuring variables within a population at a particular time.

caution: Counts need a defined population and time. No real-world percentages are claimed on this board.
question: Which concept concerns new cases during a defined period?
answer: Incidence.
sourceNote: Walker, Wood & Nicol, Mastering Medical Terminology, 3rd ed., Chapter 24, printed p. 537.

title: Decode a term: a five-step method
outcome: Find the parts, form a provisional meaning, then verify the full term.

terms.definition: Copy the exact spelling; look for familiar components.
The ending often signals a condition or procedure.
The root gives the core idea; a prefix modifies it if present.
For pericarditis: peri- around, cardi heart, -itis inflammation.
Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, the sac around the heart.

caution: Word parts suggest meaning. They cannot establish every clinical definition.
question: Does every medical term contain a prefix?
answer: No. Some terms lack a prefix and some resist useful decomposition.

title: Read the modifier: prefixes in contrast
outcome: Notice a small prefix before deciding what a term means.

terms.definition: Above normal or excessive / below normal or deficient.
Fast / slow.
Within / between.
Around / within.
Hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia describe different blood glucose findings.

caution: Confirm the whole term and its clinical context; a prefix alone is insufficient.
question: What is the difference between intra- and inter-?
answer: Intra- means within; inter- means between.

title: The combining vowel: a useful bridge
outcome: Use common joining patterns without forcing exceptions.

terms.definition: arthr/o/pathy uses o as a joining vowel.
hepat/ic usually omits the combining vowel.
oste/o/arthr/itis retains the joining o between roots.
sub/hepat/ic does not insert a combining vowel after the prefix.

caution: These are common patterns. Verify the spelling of the established term.
question: Is a joining o normally inserted between sub- and hepat-?
answer: No: sub/hepat/ic.
sourceNote: Source checks support terminology facts. MedLex examples and memory cues are original teaching aids, not frequency rankings or clinical validation.

title: Read it aloud: listen, chunk, blend
outcome: Build clear pronunciation while keeping spelling and meaning linked.

terms.definition: Check a dictionary recording or an approved pronunciation reference.
Use the reference syllables; written word parts are not always spoken syllables.
Follow the pronunciation key; stress marks differ between dictionaries.
Say it slowly, then naturally. Compare again and retrieve the meaning.

caution: Accents and accepted variants differ. Device speech is a practice aid, not an examiner.
question: Are word-part divisions always identical to syllable divisions?
answer: No. Morphological parts and spoken syllables serve different purposes.
sourceNote: Source checks support terminology facts. MedLex examples and memory cues are original teaching aids, not frequency rankings or clinical validation.

title: Know when to stop splitting
outcome: Use context and references when word-part clues reach their limit.

terms.definition: A literal split can miss the precise clinical meaning.
Parkinson disease cannot be decoded from a body root and suffix.
MRI means magnetic resonance imaging; local abbreviations can be ambiguous.
Check the sentence, body system and authorised reference; ask for clarification.

caution: Never infer a diagnosis, extent of surgery or treatment from a word fragment.
question: What should you do with an unclear abbreviation?
answer: Confirm the documented meaning using authorised references or clarification.
sourceNote: Source checks support terminology facts. MedLex examples and memory cues are original teaching aids, not frequency rankings or clinical validation.
visual: A dictionary, a puzzle piece that does not fit, a question card and a clinician reading a record. Clear stop-and-check concept.

title: Small spelling changes, different meanings
outcome: Pause at similar-looking and similar-sounding terms.

terms.definition: Swallowing difficulty / a language impairment.
Part of the small intestine / part of the hip bone.
Kidney-to-bladder tube / bladder-to-outside passage.
Blood glucose above / below the appropriate range.

caution: Compare spelling, meaning and sentence context. Ask rather than guess.
question: Which pair separates swallowing difficulty from language impairment?
answer: Dysphagia and dysphasia.

terms.definition: Surgical removal.
Incision into.
Surgical creation of an opening.
A resulting record / a recording process / visual examination with an instrument.

caution: The ending -oma alone does not establish malignancy. Verify abbreviations and complete definitions.
question: Which ending indicates removal: -ectomy or -otomy?

title: Body directions: orient before describing
outcome: Use anatomical position and the person’s own left and right.

terms.definition: Upright, facing forward, arms by the sides and palms forward.
Toward the front / toward the back.
Toward the head / toward the feet in the upright body.
Toward / away from the body midline.

caution: Left and right refer to the person being described, not the observer.
question: Is medial toward or away from the body midline?
answer: Toward the midline.
sourceNote: Source checks support terminology facts. MedLex examples and memory cues are original teaching aids, not frequency rankings or clinical validation.

title: Body directions: distance, depth and side
outcome: Describe a structure relative to a stated reference point.

terms.definition: Nearer / farther from a limb’s attachment or origin.
Closer to / farther from the body surface.
On the same / opposite side of the body.
The elbow is proximal to the wrist. Skin is superficial to muscle.

caution: A direction needs a reference. Proximal and distal do not mean simply up and down.
question: Is the wrist proximal or distal to the elbow?
answer: Distal.

outcome: Distinguish similar forms and explain why the tempting alternative is wrong.

terms.definition: Muscle.
Bone marrow or spinal cord; context decides.
Fungus.
Mucus.

caution: Read every letter. A similar sound does not establish the same meaning.
question: Which root can refer to either marrow or spinal cord?
answer: myel/o; verify the complete term and context.

One vertebra; more than one vertebra.
One bacterium; more than one bacterium.
One ganglion; more than one ganglion. Ganglions is also accepted.

caution: These are examples, not a rule for every word. Check accepted variants.
question: What is the plural of diagnosis?
answer: Diagnoses.

title: What an ending cannot tell you
outcome: Distinguish similar forms and explain why the tempting alternative is wrong.

terms.definition: Inflammation; the cause is not specified.
Tumour or mass; the ending alone does not establish malignancy.
Disease; the precise disease still needs defining.
A condition, often abnormal; verify the complete word.

caution: Word parts offer clues. They do not establish cause, severity or a diagnosis.
question: Does an -itis ending prove infection?
answer: No. It indicates inflammation; the cause must be established separately.

title: Abbreviations: clarify, do not guess
outcome: Distinguish similar forms and explain why the tempting alternative is wrong.

terms.definition: Can be misread between medicine names; write the full medicine name.
Write the intended medicine, site or action in full.
Can be read as discharge or discontinue. Write the intended word.
Use the approved local glossary and clarify unresolved ambiguity.

caution: These are error-prone examples, not abbreviations to copy into clinical instructions.
question: What should you do when an abbreviation has two plausible meanings?

title: Sign, symptom, syndrome, diagnosis
outcome: Select the term that matches the evidence and preserve its limits.

terms.definition: An observed or measured finding, such as a measured temperature.
An experience reported by the person, such as nausea.
A recognisable group of findings or symptoms occurring together.
Identification of a disease or condition using clinical evidence.

caution: A finding is evidence. A diagnosis is an interpretation supported by evidence.
question: Is a person reporting nausea describing a sign or a symptom?
answer: A symptom.
sourceNote: Facts checked against the linked references on 17 October 2026. Original MedLex teaching examples and memory cues; independent medical-editor review is pending.

title: Time course is not severity
outcome: Select the term that matches the evidence and preserve its limits.

terms.definition: Begins or develops rapidly; often relatively short in course.
Persists over a long period.
